title: Why is this task taking so long even for a graph with merely 5-6 nodes and edges?
question:
I am trying to implement the Parallelized BFS algorithm using Pyspark. I am following the material in CS246, What exactly in my implementation is making this thing take so long? Pardon me I am just a beginner.

I was trying to implement parallel BFS (reachability) on large graphs, but first decided to sanity check with a small one. I was expecting a very small runtime but it takes like a minute for 5 nodes and 3 edges.

conf = SparkConf().setMaster("local[*]")
sc = SparkContext(conf=conf)

edges = sc.textFile("try.txt")
edges = edges.map(lambda x: (int(x.strip().split()[0]), int(x.strip().split()[1]))).sortBy(lambda x: x[0])
edges.take(5)

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

edgedata = spark.createDataFrame(edges, ['src', 'dst'])
edgedata.createOrReplaceTempView("edgedata")
edgedata.cache()

# Initial reached set
reached = spark.createDataFrame([(1,)], ['dst'])
newreached = reached

while True:
    newreached.createOrReplaceTempView("newreached")

    # Expand from current frontier (no DISTINCT in SQL)
    newreached = spark.sql("""
SELECT DISTINCT edgedata.dst
FROM newreached, edgedata
WHERE edgedata.src = newreached.dst
    """).dropDuplicates()

    # Remove already reached nodes
    newreached = newreached.subtract(reached)

    if newreached.rdd.isEmpty():
        break

    # Update reached set
    reached = reached.union(newreached).dropDuplicates()
answer:
The spark SQL module (including dataframes and SQL) doesn't have a performant way of handling graph traversals. Ideally, you should use a graph-specific spark module to process graph data, such as GraphFrames for PySpark or GraphX for Scala.

The key performance bottleneck with using spark SQL is the large number of shuffle operations which must take place to explore neighboring nodes. Shuffle operations are expensive because data has to be copied and transferred between executors. In a typical spark SQL job, you would just have a small, fixed number of shuffles to join tabular data, but graph traversals can have a join take place for every frontier exploration loop, which scales with the size and density of the graph.

If you look at the explain plan, you will see a very long execution plan and many mentions of joining (shuffling) data (i.e. SortMergeJoin, BroadcastHashJoin)

reached.explain()

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[dst#14L], functions=[])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(dst#14L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=113105]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[dst#14L], functions=[])
         +- Union
            :- Scan ExistingRDD[dst#14L]
            :- SortMergeJoin [coalesce(dst#1L, 0), isnull(dst#1L)], [coalesce(dst#17L, 0), isnull(dst#17L)], LeftAnti
            :  :- Sort [coalesce(dst#1L, 0) ASC NULLS FIRST, isnull(dst#1L) ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
            :  :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(coalesce(dst#1L, 0), isnull(dst#1L), 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=112577]
            :  :     +- HashAggregate(keys=[dst#1L], functions=[])
            :  :        +- Exchange hashpartitioning(dst#1L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=112573]
            :  :           +- HashAggregate(keys=[dst#1L], functions=[])
            :  :              +- Project [dst#1L]
            :  :                 +- BroadcastHashJoin [dst#69L], [src#0L], Inner, BuildRight, false
            :  :                    :- Filter isnotnull(dst#69L)

... (similarly for 600+ lines)

As a side note, in your SQL statement, you have a cross join taking place when expanding the frontier, which does not scale well with the size of the data:

SELECT DISTINCT edgedata.dst
FROM newreached, edgedata
WHERE edgedata.src = newreached.dst

Instead, it should be more performant to use an inner join to minimize the number of records being produced by the join that spark will then have to filter through:

SELECT DISTINCT edgedata.dst
FROM newreached 
JOIN edgedata ON edgedata.src = newreached.dst
